chapter_theme: Anger is the self-destroying fire: it kills smiles and joy, burns the raft that would save a person, and returns on the one who holds it. Restraint counts only where anger could have had its way, and the one who drops it equals those who have renounced everything.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: where non-anger applies (301), the evil of anger (302-304), the harm to the angry person (305-307), the good of non-anger (308), what the non-angry gain (309), and the fruits of both (310).

301.reading: One who guards his anger where it can take effect truly guards it; where it can't, what does guarding or not guarding matter?
301.nuance: Virtue is located only where power is. Patience toward those who could crush you may be just caution, and the verse declines to count it.

302.reading: Anger is bad where it can't take effect; where it can, nothing else is worse.
302.nuance: This closes the gap left by 301, which could be misread as permission to rage where it doesn't matter. Parimelazhagar sets out why: at the strong it rebounds, and at the weak it brings both blame and sin.

303.reading: Forget anger at anyone at all; evils are born from it.
303.nuance: The verb is மறத்தல், to forget, not to suppress: the instruction asks for anger to go out of mind and not to be held down. Pope's 'trespass' moves the forgetting from the anger to the offence, which the Tamil doesn't do.

304.reading: Is there any other enemy than the anger that kills both the smile and the joy?
304.nuance: Parimelazhagar assigns the smile to the face and the joy to the heart, so anger destroys both outer and inner. He adds that renunciants have no outer enemies, which is why this inner one stands alone.

305.reading: If you would guard yourself, guard against anger; if you don't, it is yourself that anger kills.
305.nuance: தன்னையே, 'yourself and no other', turns anger's target around. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in light of curses: the ascetic who spends his power cursing loses it, so 'kills' means extreme suffering. Manakkudavar takes it as a threat to life.

positions.position: 'Kills' means intense suffering: the ascetic loses his austerity by cursing and is back in the misery of births.

306.reading: Anger, the fire that kills what it comes near, burns even the safe raft of one's own people.
306.nuance: The name சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி is a coinage for fire, 'killer of those it joins'. Parimelazhagar finds a contrast with ordinary fire, which burns only where it touches. It also matters that a raft is being burned by someone who needs it to survive.

positions.position: இனம் means fellow renunciants who teach, the raft that crosses the sea of births to release.
positions.quote: முற்றத் துறந்து தவஞானங்களால் பெரியயராய்க் கேட்டார்க்கு உறுதி பயக்கும் மொழிகளை இனியவாகச் சொல்லுவாரை.

positions.position: இனம் means one's friends, who bring one ashore from a sea of sorrow.
positions.quote: தன்னைக் கரையேற விடுகின்ற நட்டோராகிய புணையைச் சுடும்.

307.reading: The ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which can't miss.
307.nuance: பொருள் also varies: Parimelazhagar makes it a quality that displays one's power, citing Vaisesika usage, and Manakkudavar seems to take it as wealth when he speaks of loss of goods. The image is a fine one because the ground is untouched by the blow.

positions.position: The image is about certainty: the ruin can no more miss than a hand can miss the ground.
positions.quote: நிலத்தின்கண் அறைந்த அவன் கை அந்நிலத்தையுறுத்தல் தப்பாதவாறு போலத் தப்பாது.

positions.position: The image is about rebound: it is the striker's own hand that hurts.

308.reading: Even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames, not being angry, if you can manage it, is good.
308.nuance: புணரின், 'if it can be managed', is a rare concession in such a chapter. Parimelazhagar notes that such treatment would anger even sages. The commandment admits its own difficulty.

309.reading: All one has thought of comes together at once, if one doesn't think of anger in the heart.
309.nuance: The root உள் runs through the whole verse: thought, heart, not thinking. It sets one kind of thinking against another. The promise is enormous, and Parimelazhagar assigns it to the ascetic, though the verse itself doesn't.

310.reading: Those who go to excess in anger are like the dead; those who renounce anger are equal to those who have renounced.
310.nuance: Wordplay carries the argument: இறந்தார் is both 'those who exceed' and 'those who have died'. துறந்தார் doubles in the same way, so a single renunciation is set equal to total renunciation.

positions.position: They equal those who have attained release, since knowledge is certain for them though they still have a mortal body.
They equal those who have given up all possessions.
positions.quote: அதனை யொழிந் தார் எல்லாப் பொருளையுந் துறந்தாரோடு ஒப்பர்,

links.note: Both are about the moment of having power over someone weaker. 250 offers a memory that stops you: your own fear before the strong. 301 says that only at this moment does restraint count as virtue at all.

264 credits austerity with the power to crush foes. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 305, the ascetic who uses this power in a curse loses his austerity and returns to the misery of births. The power is real, but using it destroys its source.

Both distinguish the laughter of the face from that of the heart. 786 says that friendship that smiles only on the face isn't friendship, and 304 says anger kills both, so a smile alone isn't what is at stake.
Both ask for restraint under extreme provocation. 157 goes further and grounds it in pity for the wrongdoer's coming fall, whereas 308 offers no reason, only the admission that it is hard.
The same promise, that what one wants arrives as one wants it, is made for austerity in 265 and for non-anger in 309. On this comparison, dropping anger can do the work of austerity.

source_issues: 304, 309: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
304: Parimelazhagar's gloss has உவகையம் for உவகையும் and பகையம் for பகையும்.
303: Manakkudavar's entry begins with a fragment of the verse text.
